entries.what_happened: The manuscript 'Exact quantum factoring over a fixed finite gate set' (OpenAI, dated 25 September 2026; the only manuscript in this family) claims a polynomial-time uniform family of quantum circuits that, for every integer N ≥ 2, outputs the complete prime factorization of N (primes in nondecreasing order with multiplicity) with probability exactly one (Theorem 1 in the introduction; abstract). Gate count and qubit count are bounded by a fixed polynomial in n = max{128, ⌊log₂N⌋+1}. The gate set is NOT, CNOT, Toffoli, Hadamard, S = diag(1,i), their inverses and their singly controlled versions. The construction has four parts. (a) An order trial (Proposition 'order-trial') replaces the Fourier phases of Shor's order sampling by a piecewise-linear phase register and adds classical correction modes. It returns either no candidate or a multiple of the order r of a mod m, and the probability that it returns exactly r is φ(r)λ(r), with λ(d) = 2^(−⌈log₂d⌉−10). (b) A recursive process (Proposition 'process') factors N and, recursively, p−1 for each odd prime factor p. Primes are checked by a deterministic polynomial-time test (Lemma 'primality', an AKS-type variant proved in the appendix). Composites are split by gcd(a^(r/2)−1, m) using orders found by the trial. It uses K = n⁵ repetitions per transition and L = n¹⁰ transition slots. (c) Deferred filters applied after the data have been generated (Lemma 'completion', Proposition 'known-probability') make the success probability of the whole preparation exactly p* = (1−2⁻ⁿ)^(n¹⁰) > 1/2. (d) A further dyadic correction gives a preparation whose success flag has probability exactly 1/4 (Lemma 'quarter'). One exact reflection step at that known probability, which the proof of the theorem carries out itself, then yields the factorization with certainty. The manuscript states that it 'makes no claim of a classical deterministic or randomized polynomial-time factoring algorithm'.
entries.delivers: In the quantum circuit model with classical basis inputs, the claim gives the exact, zero-error, worst-case version of the quantum case: a uniform, polynomial-size family of quantum circuits over one fixed finite gate set that outputs the full factorization with probability one, with no repetition, no bounded-error guarantee and no supplied advice. It strengthens Shor's bounded-error polynomial-time quantum factoring, which the introduction cites. Restrictions: the bounds are polynomial in n with no explicit degree stated, and the body's parameters are large (L = n¹⁰ slots, K = n⁵ repetitions per transition, phase grid Q = B¹⁶ with B = 2ⁿ). The introduction says these are not intended as practical resource improvements. The result is about quantum circuits only. The manuscript's statement of the problem ('the nondecreasing list of primes whose product is N, including multiplicities') matches the list's 'outputs its prime factorization'. The manuscript does not restate the list's classical question and does not claim to settle it.
entries.remains: If the claim holds, the classical question is untouched: whether a classical deterministic or randomized algorithm can factor N in time polynomial in log N, and the classical decision version. Also left open within the quantum model: the degree of the polynomial bounds and any practical resource count.
entries.direction: proves the quantum case exactly (zero error, fixed gate set); classical case not addressed
entries.object: The explicit object is the uniform quantum circuit family itself. For each bit length it is a circuit with N in classical basis input bits, generated by a deterministic polynomial-time classical algorithm (Section 2 and the proof of the theorem in Section 6). This is an explicit construction, not an existence argument. Its classical subroutines (the primality test, the factor-tree verification and the classical controller) are compiled into the same gate set. It is not a classical factoring algorithm.
entries.doubts: (1) The identification of the implemented acceptance event, with deferred filters computed from the generated data, with the analytic event used in the probability calculation (Proposition 'known-probability') is argued in prose. The quantum-implementation step is deferred to Lemma 'records', whose proof is a short sketch ('Induction over the procedure shows that their squared norms ... equal those in the measured procedure'). The introduction calls the deferred-test identification 'the crucial argument'. (2) The primality test (Lemma 'primality') is presented as a variant of AKS. Its correctness proof adapts AKS root-counting lemmas (Lemmas 4.7–4.8 and their footnotes, credited to Lenstra, Macaj, Kalai, Sahai and Sudan), and the constants and auxiliary prime are chosen within the appendix. (3) Uniformity is defined per bit length, but the proofs of Lemma 'quarter' and of the theorem write V_N for each N and speak of 'fixed classical input N'. The text covers this in one sentence (a circuit for a fixed bit length with the input bits as controls is polynomial-time uniform), so the per-N and per-length readings are asserted to coincide rather than separately proved. (4) The polynomial degree is never stated, and the parameters are large (see 'delivers'). The text notes this itself.
